gap: No result ChatGPT got compares how much charge current each battery needs before its heater turns on: Epoch says 0.5 A, Renogy needs more than 4 A and LiTime needs 10 A in Regular mode. None of them states that Epoch's heater runs only on incoming charge, or that Battle Born's heater (about 28 W) draws from the battery itself once a charger is connected.
standout_why: I compared against three of the four cited rivals. BatteryTrail's spec database has Renogy's 'more than 4A per battery' but gives no heater wattage or threshold for any other brand. CompareFoundry has LiTime's 10 A Regular-mode minimum and Renogy's 4 A, says Battle Born's heated SKUs exist, and already sets the cycle ratings side by side (80% vs 100% DoD). BoondockMaps names no heater power source or wattage, not even for Epoch, its only heated pick. None of the three has Epoch's 0.5 A trigger or 'charge current only' wording, Battle Born's 28 W heater drawing from the battery itself, or all the thresholds in one table. Gear Ranking (cited, and it ranks Epoch first) could not be opened because of a TLS certificate error, so it may state Epoch's 0.5 A. That uncertainty is part of why I scored 1 rather than 2.
decides: The finding confirms Epoch as the pick for anyone whose cold-weather charging comes from a small source such as solar at dawn or a trickle or low-amp charger. Its heater starts at 0.5 A (about 7 W at 14.4 V), while LiTime in Regular mode needs 10 A (about 144 W of charger output) and Renogy needs more than 4 A (about 58 W). LiTime stays the value pick only if the shopper has a charger of at least 10 A or accepts its Energy-efficient mode, which heats from the battery above 20% charge. It also corrects ChatGPT's line that heaters 'require incoming charging current': Battle Born needs a charge source present to start heating, but the roughly 28 W heater then draws from the battery. The cycle-life column does not decide anything here, because CompareFoundry already lines up those ratings.
